days.title: The Cell Theory — Historical Development and Postulates
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Trace the historical development of the cell theory.
  • State the three postulates of the cell theory.
  • Explain how each postulate is supported by evidence.
  • Appreciate how technological advances in microscopy enabled the discovery of the cell.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell — the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
  • Cell Theory — the foundational principle stating that all living things are made of cells.
  • Microscopy — the technology that made cell discovery possible.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Before the Cell — A Quick Look Back

Before the 1600s, people believed that life could arise spontaneously from non-living matter (spontaneous generation). This changed when the microscope was invented.

B. The Scientists Behind the Cell Theory

YearScientistContribution
1665Robert HookeObserved cork; called the tiny compartments "cells"
1674Anton van LeeuwenhoekFirst to observe living cells
1831Robert BrownDiscovered the nucleus
1838Matthias SchleidenAll plants are made of cells
1839Theodor SchwannAll animals are made of cells
1855Rudolf VirchowCells arise only from pre-existing cells

C. The Three Postulates

  1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms.
  3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells.

D. Modern Additions

  • Cells contain hereditary information (DNA).
  • All cells have similar chemical composition.
  • Cell activity depends on subcellular structures.

pairs.right: All plants are made of cells
All animals are made of cells

scenarios.text: A scientist observes bacteria under a microscope — a single cell performing all life functions.
A cut heals because skin cells divide to replace damaged ones.
A leaf, a root, and a stem are all made of microscopic units.
A fertilized egg divides repeatedly to form an embryo.
Every organism studied — from fungi to whales — is made of cells.
A cell's mitochondria produce energy for the cell's activities.

questions.text: Who first coined the term "cell," and what was he observing?
Which postulate was added LAST, and who proposed it?
Why was the invention of the microscope important to the cell theory?

choices.label: It allowed scientists to see cells for the first time
It replaced the need for experiments

takeaways: The cell theory is the foundation of biology.
It was developed over ~200 years by multiple scientists.
Three postulates: all organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic unit of life; cells come from pre-existing cells.

days.title: The Plasma Membrane & Cytoplasm
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure of the plasma membrane using the fluid mosaic model.
  • Explain the functions of the plasma membrane.
  • Describe the composition and roles of the cytoplasm and cytosol.
  • Relate membrane structure to its selective permeability.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Plasma membrane — a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that surrounds the cell.
  • Fluid mosaic model — describes the membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.
  • Cytoplasm — the material within the cell, excluding the nucleus.
  • Cytosol — the liquid portion of the cytoplasm.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Plasma Membrane — Structure

The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

ComponentDescriptionFunction
Phospholipid bilayerTwo layers of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads outward, hydrophobic tails inwardForms the basic barrier
Integral proteinsEmbedded within the bilayerTransport, channels, receptors
Peripheral proteinsAttached to the surfaceSignaling, structural support
CholesterolWedged between phospholipidsRegulates membrane fluidity
Glycolipids / GlycoproteinsCarbohydrate chains on outer surfaceCell recognition, adhesion

B. Functions of the Plasma Membrane

  • Selective permeability — allows some substances in, keeps others out.
  • Cell signaling — receptors detect chemical messages.
  • Cell recognition — identifies the cell as "self."
  • Anchoring — connects to cytoskeleton and other cells.

C. The Cytoplasm

  • Cytosol — the jelly-like fluid (mostly water, ions, enzymes)
  • Organelles — membrane-bound and non-membrane-bound structures
  • Cytoskeleton — protein filaments providing shape and movement
  • Inclusions — stored nutrients, pigments, crystals

D. Fluid Mosaic Model — Why "Fluid"?

Phospholipids and proteins can move laterally within the membrane. Fluidity is essential for cell movement, protein function, and membrane fusion.

scenarios.text: A scientist notices that membrane proteins drift laterally within the bilayer.
Chains of sugars on the outer surface identify the cell as "self."
A molecule moves from outside to inside without using energy.
Cholesterol keeps the membrane from becoming too rigid or too fluid.
The plasma membrane lets K⁺ in but blocks Na⁺.
Everything inside the cell except the nucleus.

questions.text: Which model describes the plasma membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins?
What is the primary function of cholesterol in the plasma membrane?
What is the difference between cytoplasm and cytosol?

choices.label: Cytoplasm includes all cell contents except the nucleus; cytosol is just the fluid portion
Cytosol includes organelles; cytoplasm does not
Cytoplasm is only in plant cells

takeaways: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins (fluid mosaic model).
It is selectively permeable, controlling what enters and exits the cell.
The cytoplasm includes cytosol, organelles, and the cytoskeleton.
Membrane fluidity is essential for cell function.

days.title: Major Organelles — Nucleus, Ribosomes, ER
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure and function of the nucleus.
  • Explain the roles of ribosomes in protein synthesis.
  • Differentiate rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
  • Explain how the endomembrane system works together.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nucleus — the control center of the cell containing DNA.
  • Ribosome — the site of protein synthesis.
  • Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) — a network of membranes for synthesis and transport.
  • Endomembrane system — ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles working together.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Nucleus

StructureFunction
Nuclear envelope (double membrane)Separates nucleus from cytoplasm
Nuclear poresAllow exchange of materials (mRNA, proteins)
NucleolusSite of ribosome assembly
ChromatinDNA + proteins (chromosomes when condensed)
NucleoplasmJelly-like fluid inside the nucleus

B. Ribosomes

  • Structure: Two subunits (large + small), made of rRNA and proteins
  • Function: Protein synthesis (translation)
  • Types: Free ribosomes (internal proteins) vs. Bound ribosomes (proteins for export)
  • Found in: Both prokaryotes (70S) and eukaryotes (80S)

C. Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

TypeStructureFunction
Rough ERStudded with ribosomesProtein synthesis, folding, and transport
Smooth ERNo ribosomes; tubularLipid synthesis, detoxification, calcium storage

D. The Endomembrane System

  1. Ribosome → protein synthesized into rough ER
  2. Rough ER → protein folded and modified
  3. Vesicle → carries protein to Golgi apparatus
  4. Golgi → further modifies, sorts, and packages
  5. Vesicle → delivers to destination

scenarios.text: A liver cell detoxifies alcohol after a night out.
A cell produces a lot of digestive enzymes for export.
A cell is building new ribosomes.
mRNA exits the nucleus to reach ribosomes.
A protein is folded into its 3D shape after synthesis.
A cell needs to synthesize new membrane phospholipids.

questions.text: Which organelle is the site of ribosome assembly?
What is the main difference between rough and smooth ER?

choices.label: Rough ER has ribosomes; smooth ER does not
Smooth ER is found only in plants
Rough ER makes lipids; smooth ER makes proteins

questions.text: Which sequence correctly describes the endomembrane system?

takeaways: The nucleus houses DNA and controls cell activities.
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
Rough ER handles proteins; smooth ER handles lipids and detoxification.
The endomembrane system coordinates synthesis, modification, and transport.

days.title: Energy & Support Organelles — Mitochondria, Chloroplasts, Cytoskeleton
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the structure and function of mitochondria.
  • Describe the structure and function of chloroplasts.
  • Explain the roles of the cytoskeleton in cell shape and movement.
  • Compare energy-related organelles in plant and animal cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Mitochondrion — the powerhouse of the cell (ATP production).
  • Chloroplast — site of photosynthesis in plant cells.
  • Cytoskeleton — network of protein filaments for shape, support, and movement.
  • Endosymbiotic theory — mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from engulfed prokaryotes.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Mitochondria — The Powerhouse

  • Structure: Double membrane; inner membrane folded into cristae; interior called matrix
  • Function: Cellular respiration — produces ATP
  • Contains: Its own DNA (mtDNA) and ribosomes
  • Found in: Both plant and animal cells

B. Chloroplasts — Site of Photosynthesis

StructureFunction
Outer & inner membraneEnclose the organelle
ThylakoidsMembrane sacs containing chlorophyll
GranaStacks of thylakoids (light reactions)
StromaFluid surrounding thylakoids (Calvin cycle)

C. The Cytoskeleton

ComponentStructureFunction
MicrofilamentsThin (actin)Cell shape, movement, muscle contraction
Intermediate filamentsMediumMechanical support, anchor organelles
MicrotubulesThick (tubulin)Spindle fibers, cilia, flagella, transport

D. Endosymbiotic Theory

Mitochondria and chloroplasts likely originated from ancient prokaryotes engulfed by a host cell. Evidence: own circular DNA, own 70S ribosomes, reproduce by binary fission, double membranes.

scenarios.text: A muscle cell needs huge amounts of ATP.
A leaf cell captures sunlight to make glucose.
A cell divides and needs spindle fibers.
A cell moves using a flagellum.
A scientist finds circular DNA and 70S ribosomes in an organelle.
An organelle has stacked membranes filled with chlorophyll.

questions.text: What is the main function of mitochondria?
Which structure inside the chloroplast contains chlorophyll?
Which evidence supports the endosymbiotic theory?

choices.label: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
Mitochondria are found only in animal cells

takeaways: Mitochondria produce ATP via cellular respiration.
The cytoskeleton provides shape, support, and movement.
The endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
